comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C16-C21 regarding task performance and model accuracy. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported by Figure 1B data. OpenEval and peer reviewers agree that transformer models approach human-level performance with fine-tuning.

Complete agreement on claims C22-C24 about reading speed and specialized strategies. Both evaluations accept the behavioral findings without critique, treating the fast reading speed as valid evidence of task-directed behavior.

Strong agreement on claims C25-C29 regarding model performance progression. Peer review R3 additionally covers claims C34-C35, C37-C38 from OpenEval R4-R5, affirming the core finding that DNN attention weights fit reading patterns above baseline metrics. Both find the statistical analyses convincing.

Agreement on claims C30-C33 regarding text/task feature regression analyses. Peer review also includes C36 from OpenEval R5. Both evaluations accept the hierarchical modeling approach as methodologically sound, with peer reviewers specifically noting the strength of controlling for text- and question-based features.

OpenEval R5 addresses claims C35-C38 about DNN attention capturing information beyond basic features. Peer R3 covers overlapping claims (C35, C37, C38) as part of broader affirmation of the core DNN-human correspondence finding. Both accept the regression analyses controlling for covariates.

Perfect agreement on claims C39-C43 regarding spatial distribution of attention and question relevance. Both evaluations accept the convergence between annotations and eye-tracking as strengthening the validity of measures. Peer reviewers specifically note direct modeling of question relevance as a strength.

Complete agreement on claims C44-C47 about temporal dynamics and hierarchical control. Both evaluations accept the distinction between early and late processing stages. OpenEval notes alternative explanations aren't ruled out, but peer reviewers raise no methodological concerns.

Agreement on claims C48-C50 regarding layer-wise analyses and temporal-hierarchical parallels. Peer R7 also covers C83-C85 from OpenEval R13. Both treat the hierarchical layer analysis as a key contribution, with peer reviewers noting it makes results more transparent and helps assess task optimization contributions.

Divergence on claims C51-C59 regarding strategy development across question types. OpenEval finds evidence supported, but Peer R8 rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting that fine-tuned models fail to reproduce the differential behavior humans show for different question types in blocked presentation.

Strong agreement on claims C60-C70 regarding L1 vs. L2 reader differences. Peer R9 also includes C103. Both evaluations accept the native-L2 comparison as strengthening the study, with peer reviewers listing it as a specific strength. The efficiency interpretation is not challenged.

Agreement on claims C71-C78 regarding task-dependent attention in control experiment. Peer R10 also covers C80, C86 from other OpenEval results. Both evaluations strongly affirm this control experiment as evidence for task optimization, with peer reviewers explicitly stating it provides strong evidence.

Strong agreement on claims C79-C82 synthesizing main findings. Peer R11 also covers C87, C99-C100, C114-C115 from other OpenEval results. Both evaluations strongly endorse the task optimization hypothesis, with peer reviewers stating the work strengthens this line of research and contributes to theoretical understanding.

Agreement on claims C83-C85 regarding hierarchical layer analysis and temporal processing parallels. Peer R7 groups these with C48-C50 from OpenEval R8. Both accept the layer-wise decomposition as valid evidence for the optimization hypothesis and hierarchical attention control.

Agreement on claims C86-C87 regarding differential predictive power of pre-trained vs. fine-tuned models. Peer R10 groups C86 with control experiment findings. Both evaluations accept this as strong evidence for training-induced attention specialization across task conditions.
Additional correspondence for C87 in context of main theoretical claims. Peer R11 treats the systematic model comparisons as supporting the task optimization hypothesis that both evaluations endorse.

Perfect agreement on claims C88-C94 regarding mechanistic explanations for DNN-human correspondence. Both evaluations accept the connection to surprisal and neuroscience findings as appropriate contextualization. Peer reviewers note the work is methodologically well grounded in NLP literature.

Agreement on claims C95-C98 characterizing prior work. Peer R13 also covers C101-C102 from OpenEval R17. Both evaluations accept the literature contextualization and positioning of current findings relative to prior models as appropriate, with peer reviewers noting the substantially more high-level task.

Additional correspondence for claims C99-C100 regarding positioning of findings. Peer R11 groups these with main theoretical claims about task optimization. Both evaluations find the comparison to prior models well-documented.

Agreement on claims C101-C102 as established background. OpenEval rates C101-C104 as UNCERTAIN due to speculation about mechanisms, while peer reviewers accept C101-C102 as appropriate contextualization without raising concerns about the speculative nature of C104.

Correspondence on claim C104 regarding speculative mechanisms. OpenEval explicitly notes this is speculative and untested, rating the group UNCERTAIN. Peer R16 accepts it as an appropriate interpretive caveat, noting the speculative nature is appropriately qualified.
Additional correspondence for claim C103 regarding L2 reading literature. Peer R9 groups this with L1-L2 comparison findings. Both evaluations accept the citation-supported contextualization.

Perfect agreement on claims C105-C113 regarding reconciliation of prior inconsistent findings about DNN interpretability. Both evaluations accept the explanation based on reader proficiency and layer depth as plausible and treat this as a valuable contribution to understanding mixed prior results.

Agreement on claims C114-C115 as main conclusions. Peer R11 groups these with synthesis of findings supporting task optimization. Both evaluations find the systematic model comparisons throughout the study well-supported.

Agreement on claims C116-C118 regarding limitations and future directions. Both evaluations accept these as appropriate interpretive caveats, with peer reviewers noting the data will be useful as a benchmark for future modeling work.

Perfect agreement on claims C119-C124 regarding experimental materials and participants. Both evaluations affirm the methodological rigor, with peer reviewers specifically praising the ecological validity of the stimuli and task design as appropriate for testing the optimization hypothesis.
Additional correspondence for claims C79-C80 in context of control experiment. Peer R10 treats these summary claims as part of the evidence from the task-dependent attention analysis.

Peer R15 addresses claims C14-C15 about established NLP background, noting the work is methodologically well grounded. OpenEval does not have a separate result evaluating these background claims, likely treating them as uncontroversial context.
